questions.explanation: Without an explicit alignment, arithmetic types are right-aligned and strings are left-aligned. So the integer is padded on the left and the string on the right. The tempting `printf` habit of right-aligning everything does not apply.

options: Yes, but it throws `std::format_error` at run time
No, ill-formed: manual and automatic indexing cannot be mixed
No, ill-formed only because the argument count is wrong
questions.explanation: A format string must use either automatic indices (`{}`) or manual indices (`{0}`) throughout. The format string is checked by a `consteval` constructor, so the mistake is a compile error. It is not deferred to run time, which would only happen with `std::vformat`.

`bool` formats as text by default and as an integer with the `d` type. A `char` formats as the character by default, unlike an integer promoted by `printf`, so it prints `a`. `true 1 97` would require `{:d}` for the char.

options: No, ill-formed: the format string must be a constant expression
Yes, but a bad `f` would be undefined behavior
Yes, but a bad `f` would throw `std::format_error`
questions.explanation: The first parameter is `std::format_string<int>`, whose constructor is `consteval` and accepts only a string known at compile time. A non-constant `std::string` does not qualify, so this fails to compile. Use `std::vformat` for runtime strings, which then reports bad strings by throwing `std::format_error`.

options: Undefined behavior, since the output does not fit
questions.explanation: `format_to_n` writes at most `n` characters but reports in `size` how long the complete output would have been, like the return value of `snprintf`. That is 8 here, and only five characters were stored. It is not undefined, because truncation is the point of the function.

The `0` option pads with zeros for finite numbers, but the standard says it does not apply to infinity and NaN, which are padded with spaces. Zero padding would otherwise turn `inf` into text that reads like a different value. The default alignment for numbers is right, so the spaces go on the left.

options: Nothing: undefined behavior, since an argument is missing
questions.explanation: `std::vformat` is the unchecked entry point, and the standard requires it to report a format string that does not match the arguments by throwing `std::format_error`. The same mistake with `std::format` and a literal would be a compile error instead. The call itself is well-formed because `a` is an lvalue, which `make_format_args` requires.

The width of 10 counts the `0x` prefix, and the `0` option inserts the zeros after the prefix, so the result has ten characters and the digits `ff` at the end. The second option treats the width as applying only to the digits. Zeros before the prefix, as in the last two, are never produced.
